All methods in this family map 3D position $\mathbf{x}$, viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$, and a temporal or deformation parameter $t$ (or $\tau$) to density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$ using differentiable neural networks or feature grids [S1][S2, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly describes a method that maps 3D position (x), viewing direction (d), and a temporal parameter (t) to density (occupancy σ) and color (c). Specifically, it states that the canonical field F_Θ maps (x, d) to color and occupancy, and the displacement field G_Φ maps (x, t) to a displacement vector. The final color and occupancy at time t are retrieved by evaluating the canonical field at the displaced position x + G_Φ(x, t). This aligns with the claim that the method maps these inputs to density and color using neural networks (MLPs). Although the claim mentions 'feature grids' and '[S2]', the prompt asks if the evidence supports the claim based on the provided text. The provided text [S1] fully supports the core functional description of the method (mapping x, d, t to σ, c via neural networks). The mention of '[S2, unofficial]' in the claim likely refers to a broader family context, but the specific mechanism described in the claim is fully substantiated by the detailed description in [S1].

It further details that the training process involves optimizing a 'rendering loss' (Source [S1], Sec 2.2, stage vi) to reconstruct shapes. In the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), optimizing rendering loss inherently involves minimizing the difference between rendered pixel colors and ground truth images. The claim accurately summarizes the optimization mechanism described in the text.

The claim states that the displacement field $G_Φ(𝐱, t)$ is an 8-layer MLP with parameters $Φ$, mapping space-time coordinates $(𝐱, t)$ into the displacement vector between point $𝐱$ at time $t$ and the corresponding point in the canonical field.
